## If regression commands are unfamiliar

Use the same workflow throughout QM Intermediate. First store the fitted
model as an object, then inspect it:

```r
model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = my_data)
summary(model)
confint(model)
fitted(model)
residuals(model)
plot(model)
```

- `lm()` fits the model. The predictors are to the right of `~`, and the
  outcome is on the left.
- `summary()` reports the coefficients, their usual t-tests, the model fit,
  and the overall F-test.
- `confint()` reports confidence intervals for the coefficients.
- `fitted()` and `residuals()` return one value for each row of the analysis
  sample.
- `plot(model)` opens the standard diagnostic plots.

Give the fitted object a meaningful name. Inspect the analysis sample before
you interpret the output. If a variable in the model has a missing value in a
row, `lm()` leaves out that row without a warning, unless you tell it to do
something else. The
[Intermediate code sheet](../intermediate/code-sheet.qmd) lists the R
commands of the course in one place.

## A five-minute return-to-R check

Run this code yourself, without copying the answers from someone else:

```r
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv")
nrow(sharks)
mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
median(sharks$description_words)
table(sharks$season)
```

Then explain each output in words. If the code runs but you cannot explain a
number, your problem is with the statistics, not with the programming.

## Making figures in R

Every data figure in this textbook comes with its R code. Click
"See the R code for this figure" above a graph to open the code. You can copy the
code into a fresh R session in your course project, and it draws the same
figure. The exam never asks you to write `ggplot2` code. For the exam, the
base R commands on the code sheet are enough. Install the plotting packages once:

```r
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "patchwork"))
```

Some rules for the graphs in your own tutorials, reports, and thesis:

- **One message per graph.** State it in the caption. Remove everything that
  does not support this message (boxes, minor gridlines, decoration).
- **Counts start at zero, and a graph has only one vertical axis.**
- **Use few colours.** Take one colour for the data (`#009E73`), a second
  for a contrast or a fitted line (`#D55E00`), and grey for context. Draw
  reference values (means, benchmarks, zero lines) as dashed lines and write
  the value next to them. Colour-blind readers can tell these two data colours
  apart.
- **Put labels directly on the graph where possible** in place of a legend,
  and always name the axes with their units.
- **Choose the form that fits.** Draw a PMF as sticks with dots, a histogram
  with a stated bin width, and a model curve as a smooth line.

Three free references go further, and they are useful for your thesis.
Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund,
[*R for Data Science*, Chapter 1](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize),
explains ggplot2 itself. Healy,
[*Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction*](https://socviz.co/), shows
how to build good graphs in R from start to end. Wilke,
[*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/),
explains the design principles.
